title: A Review of Research on Artificial Intelligence Writing Feedback: Mechanisms, Learner Behaviours, and Future Directions
venue: Journal of Educational Theory and Practice
extended_summary:
This paper is not the requested direct secondary-school intervention study. Instead, it is a 2025 review article that synthesizes research on artificial intelligence writing feedback, tracing developments from traditional automated writing evaluation systems to generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The review focuses on how different forms of AI feedback work, how learners interpret and respond to that feedback, and what theoretical mechanisms may explain links between feedback, revision behaviour, and writing outcomes.

The paper discusses two broad types of AI-supported writing feedback: local linguistic feedback, which targets grammar, spelling, punctuation, and sentence-level issues, and global feedback, which addresses discourse structure, argumentation, coherence, and organization. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory, Writing Process Theory, and feedback literacy perspectives, the authors propose a conceptual framework in which feedback characteristics shape learners’ cognitive assessment and affective satisfaction, which then influence revision intention, revision depth, and eventual writing outcomes. The paper emphasizes that AI does not improve writing directly; rather, its effects depend on how learners engage with and act on feedback.

No original participant sample is reported, and the article does not evaluate a single intervention in one educational context. Instead, it references prior studies across multiple settings, with particular attention to second-language and EFL/ESL writing contexts, many in higher education. The review notes that evidence from secondary education and from underrepresented regions remains limited, and it explicitly calls for more longitudinal, process-oriented, and ecologically valid empirical studies.

The main conclusions are that AI writing feedback shows promise for improving writing quality and self-efficacy when implemented appropriately, but the field remains constrained by short-term designs, insufficient process data, overreliance on self-report, and limited theoretical integration. The authors argue for future research that uses behavioural tracking, longer-term designs, and clearer ethical and pedagogical frameworks, especially in relation to learner feedback literacy and responsible human-machine collaboration.
quality_tier_rationale: The provided paper is a narrative/systematic review and not the target empirical secondary-school study. It does not report a transparent empirical sample, intervention implementation, comparator, or original outcome data for secondary students.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper claims generally positive effects of AI writing feedback based on prior literature, but it does not provide original effect estimates for a defined population in this article, so impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI writing feedback tools, including automated writing evaluation and generative AI systems, used to provide feedback on student writing and support revision processes.
Review discusses AI writing assistants such as ChatGPT, Criterion, Pigai, and similar writing-support tools that provide linguistic and discourse-level feedback.
